analysis.one_liner: Gives tax credits and deductions to companies turning coal, oil shale, and CO2 into fuel.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on January 24, 2007 and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give a 20% investment tax credit to companies building plants that turn coal into liquid fuel, let them write off the full cost of that equipment immediately, and extend and expand a menu of tax breaks for alternative fuels, oil shale, and oil production using injected carbon dioxide. It would also let ethanol plants write off half the cost of switching from natural gas to coal. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal companies, oil and gas producers, oil shale developers, and ethanol plant owners would gain new or expanded tax credits and deductions — including a program that could certify up to $2 billion of investment in coal-to-liquid plants for a 20% credit [S2][S3]. Energy-intensive fuel producers get much faster depreciation, which cuts their tax bills [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal, oil, gas, and oil shale producers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a 20% investment tax credit for qualifying coal-to-liquid fuels projects, with a certification program capping eligible investment at $2 billion across up to 10 project sponsors [S2][S3].
Lets taxpayers immediately expense (deduct in full) the cost of coal-to-liquid process equipment and extends expensing for oil and alternative fuel refineries through 2016 [S2][S3].

Raises the enhanced recovery tax credit from 15% to 50% for oil, natural gas, and coalbed methane projects that inject carbon dioxide, and makes that credit usable against the alternative minimum tax [S3].
Expands and extends the excise tax credit for alternative fuels through fiscal year 2020 and adds liquid fuel from U.S. oil shale as a qualifying alternative fuel [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of the forgone revenue from the credits and accelerated deductions, and the public bears the environmental cost: converting coal into liquid fuel and burning coal to make ethanol increase carbon emissions relative to the fuels they replace [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill directs subsidies toward coal-to-liquid fuel, a process that releases more carbon dioxide than producing fuel from petroleum; the bill only requires that projects 'allow for' capture or sequestration of carbon emissions, not that they achieve it [S3].
Section 8 would let ethanol plants write off half the cost of converting from natural gas to coal-fired production, replacing a cleaner fuel with coal at taxpayer expense [S3].

The bill allows the enhanced recovery credit to be taken against the alternative minimum tax, so even taxpayers who owe the minimum tax receive the fossil fuel credit, adding to federal revenue losses [S3].

Supporters' good-faith case was energy security: domestic coal-to-liquid fuel and oil shale could reduce reliance on imported oil, and the bill includes screening criteria requiring projects to be financially viable and have documented markets [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's framing is energy independence, but nearly every dollar flows to coal, oil, gas, and oil shale producers through tax breaks, while the favored technologies (coal-to-liquid fuel, coal-fired ethanol plants) would increase carbon emissions. The public cost — lost revenue and worse emissions — outweighs the modest energy-security benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Lewis of Kentucky introduced the bill on January 24, 2007 with 10 original cosponsors and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S3][S5].
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred during the 110th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 12 cosponsors, 11 Republicans and 1 Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers came out ahead: the coal, oil, gas, and oil shale producers who would have received the credits never got them, and the public avoided the cost and added emissions the bill would have subsidized.

for.name: Rep. Ron Lewis
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

for.name: Rep. Lincoln Davis
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill's only Democratic cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means (Chair Charles Rangel)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote after referring it to the committee; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was overwhelmingly Republican — 11 of its 12 cosponsors were Republicans — and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it; no roll-call vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would subsidize demand for coal through a 20% investment credit for coal-to-liquid plants, immediate expensing of coal-to-liquid equipment, and tax write-offs for ethanol plants switching to coal. The public pays through forgone tax revenue and higher carbon emissions.

It would more than triple the enhanced recovery credit — from 15% to 50% — for oil, natural gas, and coalbed methane projects using injected CO2, and let the credit offset the alternative minimum tax.
Liquid fuel from U.S. oil shale would become eligible for the alternative fuel excise tax credit, extended through fiscal 2020.
Ethanol plants would get to write off half the cost of converting from natural gas to coal-fired power, cutting their costs while increasing their emissions.
